title: Galleries and Creative Studios Help
description: Show the work, make the next step obvious, and keep every inquiry attached to a real person.
html:
Let the work be mysterious. Not the website.

Short answer

A strong creative website does three simple jobs.

It shows the work well, tells people what is happening now, and gives the right visitor a clear way to respond. The website, inquiry form, email, proposal, and follow-up should feel like one path—not five unrelated chores.

A beautiful site that hides the contact button is still hiding the contact button. Taste matters. So does the next step.

Fit map

One path from first look to real conversation.

A visitor sees current work, understands whether they can visit or inquire, chooses the right next step, and reaches the person who can answer.

Behind the page, the team can see where the inquiry came from, what it is about, and who owns the reply.

Fix the public front doorConnect the handoffs

What connects

The front of house and the back room should agree.

  • Current work: exhibitions, projects, releases, or commissions have one dependable home.
  • Visits and events: dates, hours, location, access details, and ticket links are easy to use on a phone.
  • Inquiries: buyers, press, artists, and collaborators are guided to the right question instead of one mystery inbox.
  • Follow-up: each serious inquiry has an owner, a status, and a next action.
  • Ownership: the studio controls its domain, accounts, content, and exports.

Start small

Do this before buying another platform.

  1. Choose the work that represents the studio now.
  2. Write one plain sentence for each visitor type: see, visit, buy, commission, cover, or collaborate.
  3. Test those paths on a phone with someone who did not help build them.
  4. Send every form to a named owner and a backup.
  5. Set a simple follow-up rhythm the team can actually keep.

You may need a better website. You may only need sharper pages and a cleaner handoff. We trace the path before prescribing software.

Not the move

Do not turn the studio into a software company.

Skip the giant content system, the complicated sales funnel, and the database nobody wants to maintain unless the work truly needs them. The useful setup is the one the smallest real team can keep current.

What good looks like

The work stays in charge. Visitors can tell what is current. Serious inquiries reach the right person. The team knows what happened next. Nobody needs a treasure map to update the homepage.

Next step

Bring us the messy version.

Show us the site, portfolio files, event calendar, inbox, and whatever currently counts as the inquiry list. We will map what should stay, what should connect, and what can quietly leave.

Talk through the setup or start with a plain-English Tech Audit.

title: Law Firms Help
description: Make services, consult requests, ownership, and follow-up clear without pretending technology is legal advice.
html:
Your reputation should not be trapped in an old website.

Short answer

A law-firm website should help the right person understand fit and request a conversation.

It should explain what the firm handles, where it works, who the client will meet, and how to ask for a consultation. Then the request should move into a private, accountable process the team already knows how to run.

The public website is a front door. It is not a conflict check, an engagement letter, or a substitute for the firm’s professional judgment.

Fit map

Clear public information. Careful private handoff.

A potential client finds the right service, understands the limits of the page, and sends only the information the firm is prepared to receive there.

The request reaches a named owner, moves through the firm’s approved checks, and gets a documented next step.

Clarify the websiteMap the intake handoff

What connects

Trust is built across the whole path.

  • Service pages: plain descriptions help people decide whether to call without promising an outcome.
  • Consult requests: the form asks only for approved information and explains what happens next.
  • Internal ownership: a person—not a general inbox—owns the next action.
  • Firm accounts: the domain, website, email, analytics, and vendor access belong to the firm.
  • Follow-up: the team can see whether a request was received, reviewed, and answered.

Start safely

Fix the path without rewriting firm policy.

  1. List the matters the website may describe and the jurisdictions the firm may name.
  2. Have the firm approve every claim, disclaimer, form field, and next-step message.
  3. Separate public contact from any private or sensitive intake process.
  4. Test who receives each request and what happens when that person is away.
  5. Document ownership and recovery access for every account.

Little Fight can design and connect the technology. The firm and its qualified advisers decide the legal, ethics, privacy, retention, and security requirements.

Not the move

Do not pour a broken intake process into a shinier form.

A new form cannot decide who reviews a matter, what information is safe to collect, or how fast the firm should respond. Those decisions come first. Software comes after.

What good looks like

The right person can understand the practice and ask for a conversation. The firm receives only what it expects. A named team member owns the handoff. Accounts and content stay under firm control.

Next step

Start with the public path and the account map.

We can review the current website, request flow, domain, email, analytics, and vendor access. You keep the professional decisions; we make the technology easier to see and own.

title: Medical and Wellness Practices Help
description: Give people a calm path to services and appointments while keeping sensitive information in approved systems.
html:
Make getting started feel calmer than the waiting room.

Short answer

People need clarity before they need another portal.

A useful practice website explains services, location, availability, payment basics, and the approved way to request care. It hands the person to the right booking or intake system without asking the public website to hold information it should not hold.

The goal is simple: less guessing for the patient, fewer mystery messages for staff, and a clear line between public information and private care.

Fit map

Public information in front. Approved systems behind it.

A person understands the service, sees how to start, and moves into the practice’s approved appointment or intake path.

Staff can see the request, its owner, and its next step without copying sensitive details into random inboxes or spreadsheets.

Clarify the public websiteConnect approved handoffs

What connects

The useful system is boring in the best way.

  • Services: people can understand what is offered and what the page cannot answer.
  • Location and access: hours, arrival details, accessibility information, and contact routes agree.
  • Appointments: the website points to one approved source of availability.
  • Forms: public forms collect only what the practice has approved for that channel.
  • Staff handoff: the right person can see and own the next action.

Start safely

Decide the boundary before connecting anything.

  1. Mark every field or message that could contain health or other sensitive information.
  2. Ask the practice’s qualified privacy, security, and compliance advisers which systems and workflows are approved.
  3. Keep general website questions separate from clinical intake and records.
  4. Test the appointment path on a phone, including cancellations and staff absences.
  5. Document who owns each account and how access is recovered.

Little Fight can build the public experience and connect approved tools. We do not decide whether a workflow meets a practice’s legal or clinical obligations.

Not the move

Do not send sensitive information through whatever form was easiest to install.

A form that works is not automatically a form that fits. First decide what may be collected, where it may go, who may see it, and how long it should remain there. Then build the shortest approved path.

What good looks like

People can understand the practice and take the next step. Staff know where each request lands. Sensitive information stays in systems the practice has approved. The public website remains simple enough to keep accurate.

Next step

Bring the website and the real workflow.

We will map what a person sees, where the request goes, which tool owns the record, and where staff still copy information by hand. The practice keeps control of every policy decision.

Talk through the public path or start with a Tech Audit.

title: Professional Services Help
description: Turn expertise into a clear path from first question to proposal, follow-up, and work your firm can own.
html:
Your clients buy judgment. The website should make that easier to see.

Short answer

Explain the problem, show how you think, and make the next step plain.

A professional-services website should help the right client recognize their problem, understand the firm’s fit, see credible proof, and request the correct conversation. Behind that page, the inquiry should have an owner and a visible next action.

No funnel gymnastics. No twelve-field form asking strangers to do your discovery call for you.

Fit map

One line from expertise to accountable follow-up.

A buyer finds the relevant service, sees proof, understands the first conversation, and sends the minimum useful information.

The firm qualifies the request, prepares the next step, and keeps the relationship attached to a person instead of scattered across inboxes.

Make expertise clearConnect inquiry to follow-up

What connects

The website is one part of the sale, not the whole circus.

  • Services: each page names the owner problem, the fit boundary, and the next useful step.
  • Proof: approved examples show the work without inventing outcomes or exposing client information.
  • Inquiry: the form asks enough to route the conversation, not enough to punish the visitor.
  • Proposal: the team knows what was promised, who owns it, and what the client sees next.
  • Ownership: firm leaders can access the domain, website, email, analytics, and exports.

Start small

Follow one real lead through the building.

  1. Choose a recent good-fit inquiry.
  2. Write down every page, email, calendar, document, and person it touched.
  3. Circle every place the buyer had to repeat information or wait without context.
  4. Pick one source of truth for the relationship and one owner for the next action.
  5. Fix the smallest break that appears on every good lead.

That may mean a website rebuild. It may mean three better pages and a saner handoff. We show the path before we price the work.

Not the move

Do not buy a giant CRM to solve an unclear promise.

If the team cannot explain who the service is for, what happens first, and who owns the follow-up, more fields will only create a more expensive mess. Clarify the human job first.

What good looks like

A good-fit buyer recognizes the firm, sees how to begin, and reaches the right person. The team can see what was asked, what was promised, and what happens next. The firm owns the accounts.

Next step

Show us one real path.

Bring a recent inquiry, the current site, the proposal process, and the tools the team touches. We will map what to keep, connect, replace, or stop doing.

Start a plain conversation or request a Tech Audit.

title: Restaurants and Bars Help
description: Keep menus, hours, reservations, orders, events, and follow-up on one clear customer path.
html:
The regular knows the drill. Google does not.

Short answer

Help a hungry person make one fast, confident choice.

A restaurant or bar website should make the current menu, hours, location, reservation or order path, accessibility details, and contact options easy to use on a phone. Those public facts should agree with the tools staff use during service.

If the kitchen says one thing, the website says another, and the booking tool has entered its own little universe, the guest gets the bill for the confusion.

Fit map

From local search to the right table, order, or conversation.

A guest sees accurate facts, chooses dine-in, reservation, pickup, delivery, private event, or a simple call, and lands in the tool that owns that action.

Staff can see the request without retyping it into three places, and owners know which system is responsible when something disagrees.

Fix the guest-facing pathConnect the shift handoffs

What connects

One guest path. Several tools. Clear jobs.

  • Discovery: the website and public listings agree on name, location, hours, and phone.
  • Decision: menus are readable, current, and not trapped inside a blurry image.
  • Action: reservation, order, event, and call buttons go where they say.
  • Service: staff know which tool owns the reservation, ticket, or request.
  • Follow-up: reviews and event leads reach someone who can respond.

Start tonight

Test the busiest five minutes from the guest’s phone.

  1. Search the business name and compare every visible hour, address, menu, and phone number.
  2. Open the menu on a small screen and find a popular item.
  3. Try the reservation or order path without completing a real purchase.
  4. Trace a private-event request to the person who owns it.
  5. Write down which system wins when two tools disagree.

Do not replace a working POS because a website page is stale. First identify the real source of truth and repair the handoff.

When the screen goes dark

The emergency plan should fit on one page.

Document who to call, which cables and accounts belong to what, how to use the approved backup process, and what staff may do without an owner present. NYC venues can ask us about local, on-site support. Remote website and systems work is available across the United States.

What good looks like

Guests see accurate facts and get one obvious next step. Staff know which screen owns which job. Owners can recover the accounts. A Friday-night problem does not require an archaeological dig through old group texts.

Next step

Walk us through one shift.

Show us how a guest finds you, books or orders, reaches staff, and follows up. We will separate the working pieces from the handoffs that keep starting fires.

Tell us what keeps breaking or start with a Tech Audit.

title: Retail and E-commerce Help
description: Make products, prices, stock, pickup, shipping, and customer messages agree with the real shelf.
html:
The website and the shelf need to stop arguing.

Short answer

Choose one truth for every product fact.

Customers need to know what an item is, what it costs, whether it is available, how they can receive it, and what happens after they pay. Staff need the website, register, inventory, pickup, shipping, and customer messages to use the same answers.

A second online store is not a strategy. It is usually a second place to forget to update the price.

Fit map

One path from product discovery to a fulfilled promise.

A customer finds the right item, understands price and availability, chooses delivery or pickup, completes the approved payment path, and receives clear next steps.

Staff see the order in the system that owns it, update its status once, and know what to do when stock or fulfillment changes.

Clarify the storefrontConnect sale to fulfillment

What connects

Every promise needs an owner.

  • Product facts: title, price, options, images, and availability have a named source of truth.
  • Checkout: the customer knows what they are buying, how they will receive it, and where to get help.
  • Store operations: staff can see online orders without maintaining a secret second inventory.
  • Pickup and shipping: status messages match what the team can actually deliver.
  • Returns and questions: policy and contact routes are easy to find before and after the sale.

Start with one item

Follow a real product from box to browser.

  1. Pick a popular item with options, stock, or pickup.
  2. Write down where its title, price, photos, quantity, and status are edited.
  3. Place a safe test order or use a documented test mode.
  4. Watch what the customer and staff each receive.
  5. Fix the first duplicate entry or unclear ownership point.

Repeat that path before adding marketplaces, subscriptions, loyalty apps, or another dashboard.

Not the move

Do not automate disagreement.

If two systems already have different prices or quantities, syncing them faster does not create truth. Decide which system owns each fact, clean the data, and then connect only what the team can support.

What good looks like

The customer sees a clear offer and receives what was promised. Staff update product facts in the right place. Owners can see and recover the store accounts. The website supports the real shop instead of inventing a parallel one.

Next step

Bring one messy order.

Show us the storefront, register, inventory, fulfillment steps, messages, and the spreadsheet someone swears is temporary. We will map the smallest dependable setup.

Talk through the store or start with a Tech Audit.

title: Salons and Wellness Help
description: Connect services, portfolios, booking, reminders, checkout, reviews, and rebooking without calendar chaos.
html:
Clients should book the service. Not a guessing game.

Short answer

Make the path from “I like this work” to “I booked the right thing” obvious.

A salon or wellness website should show the work, explain services in everyday language, set useful expectations, and send each client to the calendar that truly owns availability. Reminders, checkout, reviews, and rebooking should follow that same client—not start a new scavenger hunt.

One clear calendar beats three clever ones arguing over Tuesday at 2:00.

Fit map

From local discovery to a confident booking and return visit.

A client sees the service, understands fit and preparation, chooses the right provider or option, and books through the approved calendar.

The team sees one appointment, knows what was requested, and can guide checkout, review, and rebooking without copying the client between tools.

Clarify services and bookingConnect the client handoffs

What connects

The booking button is the middle, not the beginning.

  • Discovery: current work, location, hours, and contact information are easy to verify.
  • Service choice: names, durations, price context, preparation, and fit are clear enough to choose.
  • Availability: one approved calendar owns the open times.
  • Appointment: reminders and changes reach the client and the right professional.
  • Return: checkout, review, and rebooking have clear next steps without pressure tricks.

Start with Tuesday

Follow one normal appointment all the way through.

  1. Search the business and compare the visible services, hours, location, and booking links.
  2. Choose a service from a phone without insider knowledge.
  3. Confirm that the right duration, provider, price context, and preparation appear.
  4. Trace confirmations, changes, checkout, and rebooking.
  5. Remove the first duplicate calendar or manual copy step you find.

If the existing booking tool works for clients and staff, keep it. A custom website can make the path clearer without replacing the calendar.

Not the move

Do not hide a scheduling problem under prettier photos.

Great work deserves great photos. But photos cannot fix double-booking, unclear service names, missing buffers, or a calendar nobody owns. Fix the promise and the handoff together.

What good looks like

New clients can choose confidently. Regulars can book quickly. Staff see one dependable schedule. Owners control the domain, site, booking links, and account access. Rebooking feels helpful, not desperate.

Next step

Show us the real booking path.

Bring the website, service menu, booking tool, reminder messages, checkout, and the notes staff use to fill the gaps. We will map what should stay and what should connect.

Talk through the client path or start with a Tech Audit.
